INTRODUCTION
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a motor function
disorder characterized by progressive rigidity and stiff-
ness predominantly of the trunk muscles with superim-
posed spasms. Neurophysiological studies reveals con-

with abnormally enhanced extereoceptive reflexes!: 2.
The pathogenesis of SPS is not fully understood. It
has been suggested that the continuous motor unit dis-
charges underlying the rigidity and spasms result from
an imbalance between excitatory (catecholaminergic)
and inhibitory (GABAergic) pathways controlling
alpha motor neurons activity!. In fact, high doses of
GABAergic agonists, such as baclofen and benzodiaze-
pines, are regarded as the most useful treatments for
SPS. Antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD), an enzyme concentrated in GABA-ergic nerve
terminals and in pancreatic f cells, are present in the
serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of approximately

Although symptoms usually begin with tightness or
stiffness of trunk muscles, they may slowly spread to
proximal limbs muscles’: ?. Recently, Brown et al®
drew attention to a new group of SPS patients who
present stiffness and painful spasms confined to the
lower limbs, with abnormal fixed posturing of the foot.
We report the case of a SPS patient with rigidity,
abnormal fixed foot posturing, and painful spasms
limited to lower limbs. The electromyographic exami-
nation disclosed CMUA of the affected muscles at rest
and abnormally segmented EMG activity during
spasms. Furthermore, she had high-titer of serum and
CSF anti-GAD antibodies. Clinical symptoms, elec-
trophysiological and immunological profiles suggest a
focal form of SPS.
CASE REPORT
A 39-year-old woman consulted for pro: ive gait instabi-
lity, painful spasms, and stiffness of both legs that started two
years ago. Her nptoms progressed, leading to a persistent
abnormal lower limbs posture with inversion of her left foot,
involuntary painful spasms with tonic extension of both legs,
difficulty in walking and unexpected falls. Past medical his-
tory was significant for policystic ovary, uterine myomas,
breast dysplasia, and hypothyroidism under treatment. Gene-
ral examination was normal. On neurological examination
there was abnormal posturing, with knees extension and left
foot inversion. Legs were rigid, prevailing distally and on the
left side, and movements were limited. Upper limb tone and
strength were normal. Osteotendinous reflexes were brisk,
predominantly in the left lower limb. The gait was very cau-
tious, she walked only with assistance, with stiffness of both
legs more severe on the left side. During spasms she could
stand but not walk. The rest of neurological examination was
normal. Results of brain and spinal cord MRI and CSF analy-
sis were normal. The following laboratory tests were unre-
markable: basic blood screen, B12 vitamin, folic acid, thyroid
90
mber of patients affected out of those tested; **four of these patients were
hormones, treponemal and HTLV-I serology. Needle elec-
tromyography disclosed continuous firing of action potentials
restricted to the tibialis anterior, quadriceps and peroneous
brevis muscles. By contrast, there was no evidence of CMUA
in the paraspinal muscles. Spasms of the legs occurred spon-
taneously and during attempted voluntary movements of the
legs. The spasms were characterized by the replacement of
the normal interference pattern by segmented EMG activity
in the affected muscles, particularly quadriceps and tibialis
anterior. There was no evidence of myotonia, pseudomyoto-
nia or fasciculations. Motor and sensory nerve conduction
studies were normal.

Anti-GAD antibodies were assessed by radioimmunoassay
and confirm by immunoblot as previously reported’. For
radioimmunoassay anti-GAD antibodies were measured with
a commercial kit (CIS Biointernational, Gif-sur-Yvette, Fran-
ce), following the manufacturer's instructions, using for the
detection '?>T-labelled human recombinant GAD65 protein.
By this technique, anti GAD antibodies were found in CSF at
a titer of 138 U/ml, and in serum at a titer of 32,500 U/ml.
The serum and CSF of the patient recognized a band in
immunoblots of GAD65 recombinant protein with the same
electrophoretic mobility as that recognized by GAD-6 mono-
clonal antibody. In contrast, anti-amphyphysin antibodies
assessed by Western blot and immunoprecipitation techni-
ques’: 9 were absent. Thyroglobulin and thyroperoxidase anti-
bodies were raised. The patient was treated with intravenous
immunoglobulin (IVIG) 400 mg/kg/day for 5 days with poor
response. Subsequently she was started on clonazepam
(4 mg/day). Within a few days she no longer complained of
spasms or stiffness and was able to walk without assistance.
At the time of submittion the patient was followed for
26 months.
DISCUSSION
SPS is a syndrome with a characteristic clinical and
electrophysiological picture defined by the Lorish’s cri-
teria', Recently a focal variant of this disease was des-
cribed® '!: stiff leg syndrome. In this group of patients
stiffness and spasms remained confined to the lower
limb. In addition, Barker et al!? boarder this concept
showing that this condition may also involve the upper
limb in some patients. Accordingly, this entity was

renamed as stiff limb syndrome. Interestingly, these
patients presented a different underlying pathophysio-
logy, natural history and prognosis, suggesting that
patients with stiff limb syndrome are different from
those with SPS!?.
We report a new patient with stiff leg syndrome. Her
clinical picture was characterized by insidious onset of
rigidity, painful spasms and abnormal leg posture, with-
out involvement of the trunk or upper limb muscles.
Symptoms and signs of brainstem, sensory dysfunc-
tion and sphincter disturbance were absent. EMG exa-
mination disclosed continuous motor unit activity at
rest, and abnormally segmented EMG activity during
spasms. The patient also had high anti-GAD antibodies
titer. The table 1 summarized the cases of focal SPS
previously published in the literature.
An autoimmune pathogenesis of SPS was suggested
by the observation that this condition is often associa-
ted with other autoimmune diseases such as insulin
dependent diabetes mellitus (IDDM), Hashimoto's thy-
roiditis, Graves’ disease, ovarian or adrenal failure and
pernicious anemia® +. Furthermore, anti-GAD antibo-
dies are present in high titers in CSF and serum of
60% of these patients, suggesting an autoimmune-
mediated impairment of GABAergic neurotransmis-
sion* 4, Although the hypothesis that GAD autoimmu-
nity might have a direct relationship with SPS is very
attractive, a significant fraction of patients with SPS
failed to present a recognizable autoimmune or syste-
mic disorder and yet exhibited all the clinical and elec-
trophysiological features of the syndrome?* + '°, Case
history comparisons of SPS in anti-GAD antibody
positive and negative patients have not revealed
obvious clinical differences between the two popula-
tions*. Moreover, anti-GAD antibodies have been
reported in up to 70% of new onset IDDM patients with-
out clinical or electrophysiological evidence of motor-
unit hyperactivity* +,
As clinically, from the immunological point of view,
it is possible to support the notion that patients with
SPS constitute a heterogeneous group! !3. 14, In a first
group, patients have a history of other autoimmune
diseases and test positive for anti-GAD antibodies, and
other organ specific antibodies. In a second group of
patients, SPS may develop as a paraneoplastic syndro-
me with autoantibodies recognizing brain proteins
other than GAD. Finally, a third group of patients has
no evidence of autoimmunity or other systemic disor-
ders that may be implicated in the pathogenesis of
their symptoms!) !3,
57
In summary, definition of the different clinical and
immunological pictures of the SPS is important, parti-
cularly when they provide information relevant for the
clinical management and prognosis of these patients.
